name: probe-rs-tools
desc: Collection of on chip debugging tools to communicate with microchips
why: Talks to debug probes over JTAG and SWD, opening a window into chips and firmware on your desk.

brief.what_it_is: probe-rs is a Rust toolkit for talking to microcontrollers through hardware debug probes. You give it a debug probe (CMSIS-DAP, J-Link, ST-Link, FTDI, ESP32 USB JTAG, WLink, Blackmagic, and others) and a target chip name, and you can flash a firmware binary (ELF, BIN or IHEX), run it, and stream RTT and defmt output back to your console. It also exposes a library API for reading and writing target memory, halting, stepping and setting breakpoints, and a Debug Adapter Protocol server for VS Code and other editors. The brew package installs three executables: probe-rs, cargo-flash and cargo-embed.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes it as 'a modern, embedded debugging toolkit, written in Rust', with the goal 'to provide a toolkit to interact with a variety of embedded MCUs and debug probes'. The homepage pitches it as 'The user-friendly & flexible embedded toolkit that just works' and promises 'Embedded programming made easy' with 'the ease of a native application'.
brief.how_it_works: The library opens a debug probe and attaches to a named chip, then talks to ARM, RISC-V and Xtensa cores over SWD or JTAG. Flash programming uses CMSIS-Pack flash algorithms, and target descriptions are generated from CMSIS-Packs with the target-gen tool. The README also says probe-rs can drive SWD directly from a Linux host's GPIO or spidev interface through a plugin crate, without a dedicated probe.

commands_seen.context: Written as the Cargo runner in .cargo/config.toml (runner = "probe-rs run --chip nRF52840_xxAA"). The README says it flashes firmware, resets the target and streams RTT/defmt output and panics back to the console. It is the recommended tool for most projects.
Plain prose in the README: once the runner is configured, 'cargo run' flashes and runs the firmware on the chip.
Linux host example: bit-bangs SWD over the GPIO character device /dev/gpiochip1, with the pin map encoded in a synthetic probe selector. The README's ellipsis stands for the rest of the command.
Linux host example: selects the spidev-based SWD backend, which emulates SWD by tying MOSI and MISO together through a series resistor.

brief.install_notes: The README recommends downloading a precompiled release and points to https://probe.rs/docs/getting-started/installation for the full guide; I did not fetch that page, so per-platform details are unverified. Building from source needs Rust and Cargo, installed via rustup. Writing a Cargo runner config is the usual setup step for embedded projects. For the Linux-host SWD mode, the README says to use the probe-rs-linux plugin crate and see its README for wiring diagrams, cross-compilation and remote-server use. probe-rs list only shows explicit /dev/spidev_swd* udev links, so those links need to be set up first.
brief.standout: Setting probe-rs run as a Cargo runner makes cargo run flash the chip and stream RTT/defmt logs in one step, so embedded Rust development feels like running a native program. Target support is also generated from CMSIS-Packs, and the Linux-host mode can turn a Linux board's own GPIO pins into an SWD probe.
brief.status: unknown. The GitHub README I fetched shows a crates.io badge, a CI status badge, a changelog/ directory of unreleased fragments and a CHANGELOG.md, which all suggest active development. I could not see a release date or last-commit date in the pages I read.
brief.caveats: The README says cargo-embed 'is expected to be phased out in the future, so prefer probe-rs run for new setups'. The Linux-host SWD mode needs hand wiring and udev setup. The homepage says the project's own open-source probe is 'coming soon'. Building needs a Rust toolchain. Licensing is dual Apache-2.0 or MIT. The homepage says the STM32 memory maps were once unreliable and now rely on stm32-data. I did not check the brew formula's notes; its caveats field is empty.

entry.title: probe-rs
entry.tldr: A Rust toolkit that flashes, runs and debugs microcontrollers through a hardware debug probe, streaming the chip's log output back to your terminal.
entry.deeper_look:
probe-rs connects to a debug probe (CMSIS-DAP, J-Link, ST-Link, FTDI, ESP32 USB JTAG, Blackmagic and others), attaches to a named chip, and talks to ARM, RISC-V and Xtensa cores over SWD or JTAG. From there it can flash an ELF, BIN or IHEX file, reset the target, and stream RTT and defmt output and panics back to your console. As a library it can also read and write target memory, halt, step and set breakpoints. It includes a Debug Adapter Protocol server so editors such as VS Code can use it.

The brew package installs three executables: probe-rs, cargo-flash and cargo-embed. The README says that for most projects probe-rs run is the one to use, and that cargo-embed is expected to be phased out. The README describes the project as "a modern, embedded debugging toolkit, written in Rust".

The usual setup is to put probe-rs run in .cargo/config.toml as the Cargo runner. After that, cargo run flashes the chip and shows its logs, so firmware on a board feels like running a native program.

Underneath is the idea that every chip has a small debug port, and a probe can use it to stop the processor, read its memory and rewrite its flash. Flash algorithms and target descriptions come from CMSIS-Packs. The README also describes a Linux mode, through a plugin crate, where a board's own GPIO or spidev pins act as the SWD probe, so no dedicated probe is needed.
entry.install:
brew install probe-rs-tools
# Needs a supported debug probe and a target board. Building from source needs Rust via rustup. The README recommends a precompiled release and points to https://probe.rs/docs/getting-started/installation.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the subcommands for working with probes and chips.
Flashes the firmware, resets the target and streams RTT/defmt output; the README uses this as a Cargo runner.
With the runner set in .cargo/config.toml, flashes and runs the firmware on the chip.

entry.whats_unique: Set as a Cargo runner, it makes cargo run flash the chip and show its logs in one step. Target support comes from CMSIS-Packs, and a Linux board's own pins can serve as the probe.
entry.caveats: It needs a debug probe and a target board to do anything useful, and the Linux GPIO/SPI probe mode needs hand wiring and udev setup.
